title: Why Every Project Should Start With Discovery
excerpt: Learn what the UX project discovery phase is, what it delivers, and how it cuts risk, scope creep, and rework before design or development starts.

mainImage.alt: Person at a desk studying user research and goals on a large screen

children.text: Most digital projects don’t fail because of bad design or bad code. They fail because the team built the wrong thing, or built the right thing without agreeing on what “right” meant. A UX project discovery phase prevents that by putting research and alignment before pixels and code.
What Is the UX Project Discovery Phase?

The UX project discovery phase is a short, focused research and planning period that happens before design or development begins. During this phase, the team defines the problem, learns who the users are, reviews competitors, checks technical constraints, and agrees on scope and success metrics.
The goal is simple: replace assumptions with evidence. By the end, everyone involved should know what is being built, who it is for, why it matters, and how success will be measured.
Why Discovery Matters Before You Build

Jumping straight into mockups feels productive. Stakeholders get something to look at, and the team feels momentum. The risk is hidden, though. Without a shared understanding of goals and users, early work often gets redone later.

Discovery turns opinions like “I think the homepage needs a video” into decisions backed by user behavior and business goals. It also gets marketers, designers, developers, and leadership working from the same picture before anything expensive is built.
What Happens When You Skip Discovery
Skipping the digital design discovery process trades a few weeks of research for months of friction. The most common problems are:
Unaligned stakeholders.

Leaders, product managers, and designers often carry different visions for the same project. Discovery workshops bring those differences out early, when resolving them costs a conversation instead of a rebuild.
Misdirected feature investment.
Teams spend budget on features users never asked for. Research shows what people actually need, so effort goes where it counts.
Hidden technical debt.
Designing before auditing existing systems, integrations, and databases leads to surprises mid-build. Problems found in discovery are far cheaper to fix than problems found after launch.
As a rule, the later an error is found, the more it costs to fix. Discovery is the cheapest point in the project to be wrong.
The Four Pillars of a Website Discovery Framework
A strong website discovery framework combines human insight with hard data. It usually rests on four pillars.
1. Business Alignment and KPIs

Every digital project should support a measurable business goal, such as higher revenue, lower acquisition costs, or fewer support requests. Stakeholder interviews clarify goals, brand positioning, and constraints. Useful questions include:
What does success look like in 6 to 12 months?
Which conversions matter most, and how are they measured?
Which internal workflows must the product support?
2. User Research and Personas

Assumptions are the biggest threat to good design. User interviews, usability observation, and analytics reviews reveal real behavior, friction points, and motivations. That research becomes personas and journey maps that guide every later decision.
3. Competitor and Market Benchmarking

No product exists in isolation. Reviewing competitors and industry leaders shows what users already expect and where there is room to stand out. Spotting where competitors create friction is often where your best opportunity sits.
4. Technical and Information Architecture Audit

Before visual design starts, review your CMS, tech stack, database structure, third party integrations, and performance baselines. This keeps technical surprises out of the build and shapes a sensible site structure from day one.
UX Discovery Deliverables That Drive Results
Discovery is not endless research. It is a tight sprint that produces practical assets the whole team can use.

cells: Defines goals, audience, and out of scope items to prevent scope creep
Shows user paths, pain points, and conversion triggers
Sets site structure, navigation, and URL hierarchy
Documents stack, integrations, data models, and security needs
Tests layout and content hierarchy before visual styling

children.text: These UX discovery deliverables act as a single source of truth, so designers and engineers can move through launch without guessing.
How Product Scoping Best Practices Prevent Budget Overruns
Budgets blow up when teams estimate costs before they understand requirements. Following product scoping best practices during discovery gives you realistic timelines and more reliable estimates.
Step 1: Prioritize Features With MoSCoW
Sort every proposed feature into one of four groups:
Must have:
Essential for launch.
Should have:
Valuable, but can follow in a later release.
Could have:
Nice additions if time and budget allow.
Won’t have:
Deliberately excluded from this phase.
Step 2: Validate Structure With Low Fidelity Wireframes
Changing a wireframe takes minutes. Rebuilding a finished component takes days or weeks. Testing structure early saves significant engineering time.
Step 3: Tie Every Element to a Goal
Each screen, form, and button should support a business objective or a user task. If an element serves neither, cut it from scope.
What a Typical Discovery Timeline Looks Like
Discovery works best as a short, structured sprint with a clear end date. The exact plan depends on the project, but most follow a similar rhythm.

cells: Kickoff workshop, stakeholder interviews, analytics and content review
User interviews, competitor benchmarking, technical audit
Personas, journey maps, information architecture, feature prioritization
Scope matrix, technical specification, wireframes, and a roadmap for the next phase

children.text: Smaller website projects can compress this into one or two weeks. Larger platforms may need extra time for technical investigation or additional user groups.
Signs Your Project Needs a Discovery Phase
Not every change needs a full discovery sprint. A small content update or a minor bug fix certainly doesn’t. But a UX project discovery phase is worth the time if any of these sound familiar:
Different stakeholders describe the goal of the project in different ways
You are not sure which features matter most to users
You are entering a new market or launching a new product
A previous version did not perform the way you hoped
The project depends on systems or integrations nobody has reviewed recently
The budget feels like a guess rather than an estimate
How to Get the Most From Discovery

Discovery is only as useful as the participation behind it. Give the team access to analytics, past research, and the people who talk to customers every day. Make decisions in the room when you can, so open questions don’t drift into the design phase. Most importantly, treat the outputs as living documents. When new information appears during design or development, update the scope and priorities rather than working around them.
How Discovery Helps Search Engines and AI Answer Engines

Search is no longer only about ten blue links. AI tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Google’s AI Overviews pull answers from content that is clearly structured and easy to interpret. Discovery sets that foundation early:
Answer Engine Optimization (AEO):
Clear definitions and direct answers give AI tools something authoritative to cite.
Generative Engine Optimization (GEO):
Well defined relationships between topics, user intent, and your expertise help AI models understand what your brand does.
Structured data:
Planning content structure during discovery makes it easier to add JSON-LD schema such as Article, Organization, and FAQPage, which helps crawlers parse your pages.

body.text: Planning a new website or product? We can run a focused discovery phase with your team.
body.label: Start a Project

faq.q: How long does the digital design discovery process take?
faq.a: Most projects need one to three weeks. Smaller website redesigns often take one to two weeks, while complex SaaS platforms or multi system enterprise projects can take three to four weeks.

faq.q: What are UX discovery deliverables?
faq.a: They are the documents and assets produced during discovery, including a problem statement, scope matrix, user personas, journey maps, information architecture, technical specification, and wireframes.

faq.q: Why do we need discovery if we already know what we want to build?
faq.a: Even when goals feel clear, team members usually hold different assumptions about the details. Discovery surfaces those differences early and grounds decisions in real user data, which prevents expensive revisions later.

faq.q: How do product scoping best practices protect my budget?
faq.a: Prioritizing features with MoSCoW, validating layouts with wireframes, and identifying technical constraints upfront removes unexpected costs and keeps the project on schedule.

faq.q: What is a website discovery framework?
faq.a: It is a structured approach to project research built on four pillars: business alignment, user research, technical auditing, and strategic roadmap planning.

faq.q: Is the UX project discovery phase only for large projects?
faq.a: No. Even small websites benefit from a lighter version. The depth of research scales with the project, but the habit of aligning on goals and users first applies everywhere.

title: Design Systems Developers Actually Use
excerpt: Learn how to build a design system for developers that teams actually adopt, with reusable components, design tokens, and clear documentation.

mainImage.alt: Design system components flowing from design files to code on laptops

children.text: A design system should make life easier for designers and developers. Too many do the opposite. They live in a Figma file nobody opens, a docs site nobody trusts, and a component library that drifted away from production months ago. A design system for developers only works when developers choose to use it. This guide shows how to build one that earns that choice.
Why Most Design Systems Get Ignored

Most design systems are built by designers, for designers. Developers receive a spec and are asked to match it. If the system is hard to find, hard to install, or slower than building a component from scratch, they skip it, and honestly, that is a reasonable call.
The usual problems look like this:
Components exist in Figma but not in code
Documentation is outdated or has no code examples
Updates ship without notice and break existing screens
There is no clear way to report bugs or request changes
The fix is not more rules. It is building the system around how developers actually work.
What Is a Design System for Developers?

A design system for developers is a shared library of reusable code, visual rules, and guidance that helps engineers build consistent interfaces without recreating UI from scratch. It combines design system components, design tokens, and design system documentation into one source of truth that connects design decisions to production code.
When it works, designers stop redlining every screen, developers stop guessing, and the product looks and behaves the same everywhere.
Start With Design Tokens
Design tokens are named values for color, spacing, typography, radius, and shadow. Instead of hard coding a hex value in forty places, developers reference a name like
color.primary
. Change it once, and every screen updates.

Tokens are the cheapest part of a system to adopt, and the payoff is immediate. A rebrand or a dark mode becomes a config change instead of a month of edits. Export them in the formats your stack already uses, such as CSS variables or JSON, so design tokens stay in sync between Figma and code automatically.
Build Design System Components in Code First

Developers trust what they can import. Build your design system components as real code in the framework your team already uses, then mirror them in Figma. Doing it in that order keeps the code as the source of truth and stops the two from drifting apart.
A few rules keep components useful:
Start small with buttons, inputs, modals, and cards
Keep props and naming predictable across every component
Make accessibility the default, including keyboard support, focus states, and contrast
Allow sensible overrides so developers never feel blocked

Well built design system components save more time than any style guide ever will. Aim to cover about 80% of real use cases and leave the rare edge cases to the team. Your first design system components should be boring and reliable, not clever.
Write Design System Documentation People Read
Good design system documentation is short, searchable, and code first. Nobody wants to read an essay before using a dropdown.
Every component page should include:
A live preview
Copy and paste code
A props table
Do and don’t examples
Accessibility notes
A changelog

Design system documentation also needs an owner. Outdated docs are worse than no docs, because they teach people to stop trusting the system. Keep the docs close to the code, with tools like Storybook or Docusaurus, so they update when the components do.
Fix the Design to Development Handoff
This is where a system pays for itself. Without one, handoff means specs, redlines, and a lot of back and forth. With one, designers and developers pick from the same set of parts.
A smoother design to development handoff comes from four habits:
Name components the same in Figma and in code
Use the same tokens on both sides
Review finished work in the browser, not just in a screenshot
Hold a short sync whenever a new pattern is introduced
A repeatable design to development handoff means fewer “this doesn’t match the mockup” comments and faster releases.
Treat the System Like a Product

The systems that last are managed like products. They have an owner, versioned releases, clear release notes, and a simple way for anyone to suggest improvements. A design system for developers grows when people can contribute to it, not just consume it.
Track a few simple numbers to see whether it is working:

cells: Share of screens using system components
Time to build a new page

children.text: Is Your System Developer Ready?

cells: Can a developer install it in minutes?
Do components exist in code, not just in design files?
Is there a way to give feedback?
A named channel and an owner
Are tokens shared by design and code?

children.text: Roll Out Your Design System in Phases
Trying to launch a complete design system in one go is one of the fastest ways to stall it. A phased rollout builds trust, because developers see value early and the system grows around real needs.

cells: Inventory existing colors, type, spacing, and components in code and design files
A clear picture of duplication and inconsistency
Consistent colors, spacing, and type across the product
Build the five to ten components used most often
Publish usage guidance, code examples, and a changelog
Developers can self serve without asking designers
Migrate existing screens and track usage
The system becomes the default way to build

children.text: Each phase should end with something developers can use immediately. If a phase only produces documents, it is too big.
Common Mistakes When Building a Design System
Even well funded teams fall into the same traps. Watch out for these:
Designing a large component library before checking what the product actually uses
Naming tokens and components differently in Figma and in code
Designing only the default state and skipping hover, focus, disabled, loading, and error states
Publishing documentation once and never updating it
Making the system so strict that developers have to work around it
Leaving ownership vague, so nobody approves changes or answers questions
Avoiding these keeps the system lean, trusted, and actually used.
Getting Buy-In From Your Team

A design system for developers is as much about people as it is about components. Involve developers from the first audit, invite them to name things, and ship improvements they asked for early on. When engineers see their own feedback in the system, they stop seeing it as a design team project and start treating it as shared infrastructure.
How a Strong System Supports SEO and AI Search

A well built design system for developers also helps your search performance. Consistent design system components output clean, semantic HTML, proper heading order, and accessible markup. That makes pages easier for search engines and AI answer tools to read, and shared components keep pages fast and consistent at scale.

body.text: Want a design system your developers will actually use? We can audit your product and build one with your team.
body.label: Start a Project

faq.q: What is a design system for developers?
faq.a: It is a shared library of reusable components, rules, and documentation that lets engineers build consistent interfaces faster, with design and code working from the same source of truth.

faq.q: How long does it take to build a design system?
faq.a: A small starter system with tokens and a handful of core components can be ready in four to eight weeks. Larger systems grow over time and are never truly finished, which is why ownership matters.

faq.q: What are design tokens and why do they matter?
faq.a: Design tokens are named values for color, spacing, type, and other style choices. They matter because one change updates every screen, which makes rebrands, themes, and dark mode far easier.

faq.q: Does a small team need design system components?
faq.a: Yes, in a lighter form. Even a small set of shared components cuts repeat work and keeps the product consistent as the team grows.

faq.q: What should design system documentation include?
faq.a: Live previews, copy and paste code, props, usage guidance, accessibility notes, and a changelog. Keep it short and keep it current.

faq.q: How do you improve design to development handoff?
faq.a: Share the same names and tokens in design and code, review work in the browser, and agree on what “done” means before development starts.

title: 5 Common UX Problems We Look For First
excerpt: Learn the five common UX problems that quietly kill conversions, how to spot them in a UX audit, and the simple fixes that win back lost customers.

mainImage.alt: Five numbered UX problems around a website on a laptop

children.text: Most websites don’t lose customers because of one dramatic failure. They lose them through small moments of friction: a button that isn’t clear, a page that loads a second too slowly, a form that asks one question too many. These common UX problems rarely show up in a design review, because the team knows the product too well to notice them. Customers notice immediately, and they leave.

When we run a UX audit, we don’t start with colours or fonts. We start with the five problems that cost conversions most often. This guide explains each one, how to spot it, and how to fix it without a full redesign.
What Are Common UX Problems?

Common UX problems are recurring usability issues that make it harder for people to understand a page, find what they need, or complete a task. They are not bugs in the technical sense. The site works, but it works against the visitor.

They matter because every point of confusion adds effort, and people have very little patience for effort online. A visitor who has to think about what to do next is a visitor who is already looking for the back button. Fixing these issues is one of the most reliable forms of conversion rate optimization, because it removes obstacles instead of trying to persuade people past them.
Why Small UX Issues Have a Big Impact

A single usability issue rarely looks serious on its own. The problem is that they stack. A slow page makes people impatient. An unclear button makes them hesitate. A long form gives them a reason to stop. Each step loses a share of visitors, and the losses multiply across the journey.
That is also why small fixes can produce outsized results. Removing friction at the busiest step of the journey helps every visitor who passes through it, every day.
1. The Main Action Isn’t Clear

Visitors decide within seconds whether a page is for them and what to do next. If a page has three buttons of equal weight, or the main button says something vague like “Learn more”, people hesitate. Hesitation turns into exits.
Signs this is happening:
Visitors scroll the whole page without clicking anything
Clicks are spread evenly across several buttons
Heatmaps show attention on navigation instead of the main call to action
How to fix it:
Give each page one main action and make it the most visible button
Use a label that says exactly what happens, such as “Book a call” or “Get a quote”
Repeat the main action after key sections on long pages
Reduce competing links near the primary button
2. Pages Load Slowly, Especially on Phones

More than half of web traffic now comes from mobile devices, often on mobile data. A page that feels instant on office Wi-Fi can take several seconds to show anything on a phone. Large images, too many font files, and third party scripts are the usual causes.

Google measures this through Core Web Vitals. Largest Contentful Paint, which tracks how quickly the main content appears, is considered good at 2.5 seconds or less. If your key pages are well above that on mobile, speed is costing you visitors before they read a word.
How to fix it:
Compress images and serve modern formats such as WebP or AVIF
Serve smaller images to smaller screens
Remove scripts that nobody uses, and load the rest after the page is usable
Test with Google PageSpeed Insights on the mobile setting
Our guide to
website speed optimization
covers this in more detail.
3. Forms Ask for Too Much, Too Early

Every field in a form is a small request. Ask for too many, and people decide the effort isn’t worth it. We often see contact forms that ask for company size, budget, phone number, and a detailed brief before someone has even decided to talk to you.
How to fix it:
Ask only for what you need to take the next step
Mark optional fields clearly, or remove them
Show errors next to the field, in plain language, as soon as they happen
Keep the button label specific, such as “Send my request” instead of “Submit”
Split long forms into short steps with a visible progress indicator
A form is a conversation. The first message should be easy to reply to.
4. Navigation Uses Internal Language

Teams name things the way they think about them internally: product codes, department names, or clever brand terms. Visitors look for the words they already use. If they can’t find “Pricing” or “Services” in your menu, they assume you don’t offer it.
How to fix it:
Use plain, familiar labels for main navigation items
Read support emails and sales call notes to learn the words customers use
Keep the main menu short, ideally five to seven items
Test labels with a quick card sorting or tree testing exercise
5. Text Is Hard to Read

Light grey text on white, small font sizes, and very long lines all make reading harder, especially on phones and for older visitors. Low contrast is also an accessibility issue. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines ask for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal body text and 3 to 1 for large text.
How to fix it:
Check text contrast with a free tool such as the WebAIM contrast checker
Use at least 16 pixels for body text on mobile
Keep lines to roughly 60 to 80 characters on desktop
Break long paragraphs into shorter ones with clear subheadings
UX Audit Checklist: The Five Problems at a Glance

cells: One primary button with a specific label
Largest Contentful Paint above 2.5 seconds on mobile
Compress images and defer extra scripts
High drop-off on the form step
Visitors use search for basic pages
Rename menu items in customer language
Low contrast or small type on mobile
Meet WCAG contrast and use 16px or larger body text

children.text: How to Prioritize UX Fixes

You can’t fix everything at once, and you don’t need to. A simple way to decide what comes first is to score each issue on two questions: how many people does it affect, and how badly does it block them?
List every issue you find, along with the page or step where it happens.
Note how much traffic reaches that page or step.
Rate how severe the issue is, from a minor annoyance to a complete blocker.
Fix high traffic, high severity issues first.
Measure the result before moving to the next fix.
This keeps effort focused where it pays back fastest, and it gives you clear evidence of what worked.
UX Best Practices to Prevent These Problems
Fixing problems is good. Preventing them is better. A few habits keep common UX problems from creeping back in:
Test new pages with a handful of real users before launch
Check every important page on a real phone, not only in a desktop browser
Review analytics monthly for pages with unusual drop-off
Keep a shared design system so buttons, forms, and text styles stay consistent
Treat performance as a feature, with a budget for page weight and load time
How Fixing UX Problems Supports SEO and AI Search

Good UX and good search performance overlap more than most teams expect. Faster pages score better on Core Web Vitals, which are part of Google’s page experience signals. Clear headings, readable text, and logical structure make it easier for search engines and AI answer tools to understand what a page is about and quote it accurately. When people find what they need quickly, they also stay longer and engage more, which sends positive signals about the page.

body.text: Want a second pair of eyes on your website or app? We run focused UX audits with a clear, ranked list of fixes.
body.label: Start a Project

faq.q: What are the most common UX problems on websites?
faq.a: The five we see most often are an unclear main action, slow pages on mobile, forms that ask for too much, navigation that uses internal language, and text that is hard to read because of low contrast or small sizes.

faq.q: How do I know if my website has UX problems?
faq.a: Look for pages with high traffic but low conversions, high exit rates on key steps, and repeated questions in support emails. Then watch a few real people try to complete a task. Where they hesitate is where the problems are.

faq.q: How long does a UX audit take?
faq.a: A focused audit of a marketing website usually takes three to five working days. A product with many flows can take one to two weeks. The result is a ranked list of problems with suggested fixes.

faq.q: Do I need a redesign to fix UX problems?
faq.a: Usually not. Most common UX problems can be fixed with targeted changes to copy, layout, forms, and performance. A redesign makes sense only when the structure of the site no longer fits the business.

faq.q: Which UX problem should I fix first?
faq.a: Start with the issue on your most visited page that blocks the main action. That is usually a confusing call to action, a slow page, or a long form.

faq.q: How do I measure whether a UX fix worked?
faq.a: Record the conversion rate, completion rate, or drop-off for the affected step before the change, ship one fix at a time, and compare the same numbers over a similar period afterwards.

title: How To Write A Brand Positioning Statement
excerpt: Learn how to write a brand positioning statement that defines your audience, your difference, and your proof, with a simple template and a worked example.

mainImage.alt: Branding moodboard with colour swatches and type samples

children.text: Before you design a logo, rewrite a website, or plan a campaign, you need to know what your brand stands for and who it is for. A brand positioning statement captures that in one or two sentences. Customers will never read it. Your team will use it every day, because it settles questions about design, messaging, and even which clients to pursue.
This guide explains what a positioning statement is, gives you a template that works, and walks through each part with practical advice and an example.
What Is a Brand Positioning Statement?

A brand positioning statement is a short internal description of the space your brand wants to own in a customer’s mind. It defines four things: the audience you serve, the need you meet, how you are different from the alternatives, and the proof that makes your claim believable.

It is not a mission statement, which describes why the company exists, and it is not a tagline, which is written for the public. It sits between strategy and execution, turning business decisions into a clear brief that everyone who writes, designs, or sells for the brand can follow.
Why Your Brand Needs One

Without clear positioning, every brand decision becomes a matter of opinion. One person wants the homepage to talk about price, another about quality, a third about innovation. The result is a brand that says a little about everything and nothing memorable about anything.
A strong positioning statement helps in practical ways:
Designers use it to choose the tone of the visual identity
Writers use it to decide what to say first on every page
Sales teams use it to explain quickly why you are different
Leadership uses it to judge new products, partnerships, and campaigns
It is the foundation of any brand strategy framework, because every later choice can be checked against it.
A Positioning Statement Template That Works
The most widely used structure comes from Geoffrey Moore’s book
Crossing the Chasm
. It is simple, and that is its strength. Each part forces a decision you might otherwise avoid.
For [target audience] who [need or problem], [brand] is the [category] that [main benefit]. Unlike [main alternative], we [key difference], because [reason to believe].
Fill it in slowly. The first draft will be too broad. That is normal.
How to Fill In Each Part
Target Audience

Pick one specific group. “Small businesses” is too broad. “Founders of early stage SaaS companies preparing their first funding round” gives you someone to design for. You can still serve others. You are simply choosing who to speak to first.
Need or Problem

Describe the problem in your customer’s words, not yours. Listen to sales calls, read reviews, and look at the questions people ask before they buy. The language you find there is usually more persuasive than anything written in a meeting.
Category

Name the category people already understand: design studio, accounting software, coffee subscription. If you invent a new category, people have to work out what you are before they can decide whether they want it.
Main Benefit
Choose the one outcome customers care about most. Not a list of features, but a result: launch faster, save hours every week, look established from day one.
Main Alternative and Key Difference

Name what customers would choose if you didn’t exist. That might be a competitor, a freelancer, an in-house team, or doing nothing. Then state the one thing you do differently that matters to them. This is the heart of brand differentiation.
Reason to Believe
Back up the benefit with something concrete: a process, a team, results, years of focus, or a specific guarantee. Without proof, a benefit is only a claim.
Positioning Statement Checklist

cells: Founders of early stage SaaS companies
Need to look credible to investors and first customers
Brand, UX, and development in one team
A repeatable launch process used on every project

children.text: A Worked Example
Here is a complete statement for a made up studio called Northlight:

For founders of early stage SaaS companies who need to look credible to investors and first customers, Northlight is the product design studio that turns rough prototypes into launch ready products in weeks. Unlike freelancers working alone, we bring brand, UX, and development together in one team, because we use the same proven launch process on every project.
Notice what it leaves out. It doesn’t mention every service, every industry, or every value. It makes one clear promise to one clear audience.
Brand Positioning Examples: Common Mistakes
When teams share their first draft, the same issues appear again and again:
Trying to serve everyone, which means the statement speaks to no one
Listing several benefits instead of choosing the most important one
Using vague words like “innovative”, “quality”, or “passionate” that any brand could claim
Describing what you do instead of what the customer gets
Making claims with no proof behind them
A useful test: if your statement would still be true after swapping in a competitor’s name, it isn’t positioning yet. Keep narrowing until it only fits you.
How to Test Your Positioning Statement
Before you build anything on it, check that it holds up:
Read it to three or four real customers. If they say “that’s exactly us”, you are close.
Ask your sales team whether it matches the reasons people actually buy.
Compare it side by side with your two closest competitors’ websites.
Check that every word is specific enough to guide a design or copy decision.
Rewrite it until it passes all four checks.
Where Your Positioning Goes Next

Once the statement is agreed, it becomes the brief for almost everything else. It shapes your tagline, the first lines of your homepage, your visual identity, the way you introduce yourself in a pitch, and which projects you say yes to. Share it with everyone who represents the brand, and revisit it whenever the business changes direction.
Brand Positioning vs Brand Messaging

Positioning and messaging are closely related, but they do different jobs. Positioning is the strategic decision about where your brand stands. Messaging is how you express that decision to different audiences in different places.
Get the positioning right first. Messaging written without it tends to drift, because every writer fills the gap with their own interpretation of what the brand stands for.

A practical way to connect the two is a simple message house. Put the positioning statement at the top, add three supporting messages underneath it, and list the proof points for each. Every headline, sales email, and social post can then be checked against that one page.
How Clear Positioning Supports SEO and AI Search

Clear positioning also makes your brand easier for search engines and AI answer tools to understand. When your website consistently describes the same audience, category, and benefit, those tools can connect your brand to the right questions and recommend it more confidently. Vague, inconsistent messaging does the opposite. It leaves machines, like people, unsure what you actually do.

faq.q: What is a brand positioning statement?
faq.a: It is a short internal statement that describes who your brand serves, what need it meets, how it is different from alternatives, and why people should believe it. Teams use it to keep marketing, design, and sales consistent.

faq.q: Is a positioning statement the same as a tagline?
faq.a: No. A positioning statement is internal and can be a sentence or two long. A tagline is a short public line inspired by it. Write the positioning first, then the tagline.

faq.q: How long should a positioning statement be?
faq.a: One to three sentences. If it needs a paragraph, it is usually trying to cover too many audiences or benefits at once.

faq.q: How often should we update our brand positioning?
faq.a: Review it once a year, or whenever your audience, product, or competitors change significantly. Strong positioning often lasts several years with only small refinements.

faq.q: Can one company have more than one positioning statement?
faq.a: You can have one company level statement and more specific statements for individual products or audiences, as long as they all support the main one.

faq.q: Who should be involved in writing it?
faq.a: Founders or leadership, someone close to customers such as sales or support, and the people who will use it most, usually marketing and design. Keep the group small so decisions are quick.

title: Usability Testing On A Small Budget
excerpt: Learn how to run usability testing on a budget with five users, a simple script, and remote tools, then turn what you see into clear design fixes.

mainImage.alt: Person testing an app prototype on a phone

children.text: Usability testing sounds like something only large companies can afford: research labs, one way mirrors, and specialist teams. In reality, the most useful version costs very little. If you can run a video call and share a prototype, you can run usability testing on a budget and learn more in an afternoon than in weeks of internal debate.
This guide shows you how to plan, run, and learn from a small usability study, step by step.
What Is Usability Testing?

Usability testing is a research method where real people try to complete realistic tasks with your website, app, or prototype while you observe. The goal is not to ask whether they like the design. It is to see where they succeed, where they hesitate, and where they get stuck.
It is one of the most direct user testing methods available, because it replaces opinions with evidence. Instead of arguing about whether a button is clear, you watch five people try to find it.
Why Usability Testing on a Budget Works
Teams often delay testing because they think it needs a large sample, special equipment, or a dedicated researcher. None of these is required for useful results.

Nielsen Norman Group has long recommended testing with around five users per round. Small groups tend to reveal most of the obvious problems, and running several small rounds as you improve the design is more useful than one large study. Combined with free or low cost video tools, that makes usability testing one of the best value activities in any project.
What You Need to Get Started
A clickable prototype or a working version of the product
A video call tool that lets participants share their screen
Five people who match your real users
A short usability test script with three to five tasks
One person to lead the session and, ideally, one to take notes
A simple thank you for participants, such as a gift card
How Many Users to Test

cells: Finds the most obvious problems quickly
Different groups often struggle in different places
Confirms fixes and catches new issues
Enough sessions to see a real difference

children.text: Step 1: Recruit the Right People

Testing with colleagues or friends is better than nothing, but they already know too much. Look for people who match your audience: existing customers, people from your mailing list, or users recruited through a testing service.

A short screener helps you avoid the wrong participants. Ask one or two questions that confirm they fit, such as their role, how often they shop online, or which tools they already use. Schedule a couple of backups, because some people will cancel.
Step 2: Write a Usability Test Script
A usability test script keeps sessions consistent, so you can compare what different people did. It usually has four parts:
A short introduction explaining that you are testing the design, not the person
A few warm up questions about their background
Three to five realistic tasks
A few closing questions about their overall experience

Good tasks describe a goal, not the steps. Instead of “Click Pricing and choose the middle plan”, say “You run a team of ten. Find out how much this would cost you each month.” That way you see how people actually look for information.
Step 3: Run the Session
Introduce yourself, ask for permission to record, and remind the participant there are no wrong answers. Ask them to think out loud as they work. Then give the first task and stay quiet.

The hardest part of usability testing is not helping. When someone gets stuck, resist the urge to explain. Instead ask neutral questions like “What are you looking for?” or “What would you expect to happen?” Most sessions take 30 to 45 minutes.
Note where people:
Hesitate before clicking
Click something unexpected first
Use words that differ from your labels
Say they expected to find something that isn’t there
Give up or ask for help
Remote Usability Testing vs In Person

Remote usability testing has become the default for most teams, and for good reason. It is cheaper, faster to schedule, and lets you reach people anywhere. In person sessions still have a place, especially for physical products, complex workflows, or audiences who are less comfortable with technology.

cells: Depends on participant’s connection and setup
No chance to ask follow up questions
More time and cost per session

children.text: Step 4: Turn Notes Into Fixes

After all five sessions, list every problem you observed and how many people ran into it. Group similar issues together, then rank them by frequency and severity. A problem that stopped three people from finishing a task matters more than a cosmetic issue one person mentioned.

Fix the top three issues first, then test again with a new group. Each round makes the product noticeably easier to use, and the improvements are easy to show to stakeholders because you have recordings of the before.
Common Mistakes to Avoid
Leading participants with questions like “Was that easy?”
Testing only with internal staff or friends
Writing tasks that give away the answer in their wording
Running one big study instead of several small rounds
Collecting findings but never scheduling the fixes
Simple Usability Metrics to Track
Watching sessions gives you the most insight, but a few simple measures help you compare rounds and show progress to stakeholders. You don’t need specialist software to record them.

cells: Whether people can complete the task at all
Mark each task as completed, completed with help, or failed
How much effort the task takes
Note start and end times from the recording
Where people go the wrong way
Count wrong clicks, dead ends, and restarts
Ask people to rate each task from 1 (very hard) to 7 (very easy)

children.text: With only five participants, treat these numbers as signals rather than statistics. Their real value is in comparison. If task success improves and ease ratings rise after a redesign, you have clear evidence the changes worked.
Sharing Findings With Your Team

Findings only matter if they lead to changes. Keep your report short: the top problems, a short video clip of each one, and a recommended fix. Watching a real person struggle is far more persuasive than any written summary, so invite stakeholders to observe at least one live session whenever possible.
How Usability Testing Supports SEO and AI Search

Pages that are easy to use tend to perform better in search too. When people find what they need quickly, they stay longer and are less likely to bounce back to the results page. Usability testing also reveals the exact words people use to describe their problems, which is valuable for headings, page titles, and FAQ content that search engines and AI answer tools can match to real questions.

faq.q: How many users do I need for a usability test?
faq.a: Five people per round is a good starting point. Nielsen Norman Group research found that small groups uncover most of the common problems, and several small rounds teach you more than one large study.

faq.q: How much does usability testing cost?
faq.a: A basic remote round can cost little more than participant incentives and a few hours of team time. Costs rise if you use a recruiting service, test with specialist audiences, or hire an external researcher.

faq.q: Can I test before anything is built?
faq.a: Yes. Testing a clickable prototype is one of the cheapest ways to find problems, because changing a prototype takes minutes while changing built code takes days.

faq.q: Should I pay participants?
faq.a: Yes. A small thank you such as a gift card shows respect for their time and makes recruiting much easier. The right amount depends on your audience and region.

faq.q: What is the difference between moderated and unmoderated testing?
faq.a: In moderated testing, a facilitator runs each session live and can ask follow up questions. In unmoderated testing, participants complete tasks on their own while software records them. Moderated sessions give richer insight; unmoderated ones are faster to run at scale.

faq.q: How often should we run usability tests?
faq.a: Little and often works best. A small round every few weeks during design and development catches problems while they are still cheap to fix.

title: What Makes A Website Load Fast
excerpt: Learn the website speed optimization steps that matter most, from images and fonts to scripts and Core Web Vitals, and how to keep your site fast.

mainImage.alt: Website speed dashboard on a laptop screen

children.text: A fast website feels trustworthy. A slow one feels broken, even when everything technically works. Speed affects how long people stay, whether they buy or enquire, and how search engines rank your pages. The good news is that most slow websites share the same few causes, and website speed optimization usually doesn’t require a rebuild.
This guide explains how speed is measured, what slows sites down most, and the practical steps that make the biggest difference.
What Is Website Speed Optimization?

Website speed optimization is the process of making pages load, respond, and settle as quickly as possible for real visitors. It covers everything from image sizes and font loading to scripts, caching, and hosting.

The goal is not a perfect score in a testing tool. It is a page that shows its main content quickly, reacts instantly when someone taps or clicks, and doesn’t jump around while it loads, on the devices and connections your visitors actually use.
Why Speed Matters for Users and Revenue

People judge a website within moments of arriving. If the page is blank or shifting, many leave before it finishes loading, and they rarely come back. Slow pages also make every later interaction feel heavier, from browsing products to completing a form.

Speed matters most on mobile, where more than half of web traffic now happens, often on slower connections and less powerful devices. A site that feels fine on a new laptop can be frustrating on a mid range phone.
How Google Measures Speed: Core Web Vitals
Google uses three Core Web Vitals to measure real world page experience:

cells: How quickly the main content appears
How quickly the page responds to taps and clicks
How much the layout moves while loading

children.text: Interaction to Next Paint replaced the older First Input Delay metric in March 2024. You can check all three in Google PageSpeed Insights, which shows lab results for any page and real visitor data for pages with enough traffic. Always start with the mobile results.
1. Optimize Images
Images are the most common reason a page is slow. A single photo straight from a camera or stock library can be several megabytes, far more than a phone needs.
Image optimization steps that make the biggest difference:
Use modern formats such as WebP or AVIF
Serve different sizes for different screens with srcset, so phones don’t download desktop images
Compress images to the lowest quality that still looks sharp
Lazy load images below the first screen
Set a width and height on every image so the layout doesn’t jump
Load the main hero image early, because it is often the Largest Contentful Paint element
2. Load Fonts Efficiently
Custom fonts make a brand recognisable, but each weight and style is another file to download. Many sites load six or more font files when two or three would do.
Use only the weights you actually need
Host fonts on your own domain where possible
Preload the main font so text appears quickly
Use font-display: swap so text is visible while fonts load
Consider system fonts for supporting text
3. Control Third Party Scripts

Every analytics tool, chat widget, heatmap, and advertising pixel adds JavaScript that competes with your own page for the browser’s attention. Over time these build up, and they are a common reason for poor responsiveness scores.
List every third party script and remove the ones nobody uses
Load non essential scripts after the page is usable
Split large scripts so each page loads only what it needs
Review tag manager containers every few months
Tag managers make it easy to add tools without a developer. That is useful, but it is also how many sites slowly get slower.
4. Prevent Layout Shifts

Few things are more frustrating than tapping a button just as the page jumps and you hit something else. Layout shifts usually come from images without dimensions, banners or embeds that load late, and fonts that change size when they arrive. Reserve space for anything that loads after the first paint, and avoid inserting content above what people are already reading.
5. Improve Hosting and Caching
Once the page itself is lean, look at how it is delivered:
Enable compression such as Gzip or Brotli on the server
Set long cache lifetimes for images, fonts, and versioned files
Use a content delivery network to serve files from locations close to visitors
Serve static HTML where possible instead of building pages on every request
Static pages, like the ones we build for most marketing websites, are especially easy to serve quickly and cheaply.
Website Speed Optimization Checklist

cells: Modern formats, correct sizes, lazy loading
Two or three files, preloaded, swap enabled

children.text: How to Keep Your Site Fast

Speed tends to slip over time as new features, images, and tools are added. The easiest way to protect it is to set a performance budget, such as a maximum page weight and a minimum PageSpeed score for key templates, and check it before every release. It is far easier to keep a site fast than to make a slow one fast again.
How to Test Website Speed the Right Way
Speed tests are only useful if they reflect what real visitors experience. A few habits make your results more reliable:
Test on mobile first.
Mobile results are usually slower and closer to what most visitors see.
Know lab data from field data.

Lab data in PageSpeed Insights comes from a simulated test. Field data, shown for pages with enough traffic, comes from real Chrome users over the previous 28 days. When they disagree, field data reflects reality.
Test key templates, not just the homepage.
Product pages, articles, and landing pages often have different problems.
Run tests more than once.
Results vary slightly between runs, so look for consistent patterns rather than single scores.
Test on a real device.
A mid range phone on a mobile connection is a useful reality check.
Who Should Own Website Speed

Speed problems often fall between teams. Marketing adds tracking tools, designers add large images, and developers add features, and nobody is responsible for the combined result. Give one person clear ownership of performance, agree a simple budget, and review it whenever new tools or templates are added. That small step prevents most slowdowns from happening in the first place.

A simple performance budget might say that key pages stay under a set total weight, load no more than a fixed number of third party scripts, and keep Largest Contentful Paint at 2.5 seconds or less on mobile. Write the budget down, share it with everyone who can change the site, and treat a broken budget like any other bug that needs fixing before release.
How Website Speed Supports SEO and AI Search

Core Web Vitals are part of Google’s page experience signals, so faster pages have an advantage when content quality is similar. Speed also helps crawlers. Lightweight, well structured pages are quicker for search engines and AI tools to fetch and interpret, which makes it easier for your content to be indexed, understood, and cited.

body.label: Start a Project

faq.q: What are Core Web Vitals?
faq.a: They are three measures Google uses to assess page experience: Largest Contentful Paint for loading (2.5 seconds or less is good), Interaction to Next Paint for responsiveness (200 milliseconds or less), and Cumulative Layout Shift for visual stability (0.1 or less).

faq.q: Does website speed affect SEO?
faq.a: Yes. Page experience, including Core Web Vitals, is one of many signals Google uses. Speed also affects bounce rates and conversions directly, which often matters even more than rankings.

faq.q: What is a good PageSpeed Insights score?
faq.a: A score of 90 or above is considered good. The score is a lab estimate, though. The real-user Core Web Vitals data shown for busier pages is a better guide to what visitors actually experience.

faq.q: What slows down a website the most?
faq.a: Large images, too many font files, and heavy third party scripts such as chat widgets, trackers, and ad tags are the most common causes.

faq.q: Is my hosting the reason my site is slow?
faq.a: Sometimes, but usually not first. Fix images, fonts, and scripts, then look at hosting, caching, and a content delivery network.

faq.q: How often should we check website speed?
faq.a: Check key pages after every significant release and review them at least monthly. Speed tends to slip gradually as new content and tools are added.

title: How To Scope An MVP Without Overbuilding
excerpt: Learn how to scope an MVP that tests one clear idea, with a simple feature prioritization method, a realistic timeline, and the metrics that prove it works.

mainImage.alt: Product team planning features on a board

children.text: A minimum viable product is meant to be small. Yet many first versions take a year to build, cost far more than planned, and launch with features nobody uses. The cause is almost always the same: the team tried to build a smaller version of everything instead of a complete version of one thing. Knowing how to scope an MVP is the skill that prevents this.
This guide walks through a practical process for deciding what goes into your first version, what waits, and how you will know whether it worked.
What Is an MVP?

An MVP, or minimum viable product, is the smallest version of a product that can test your most important assumption with real users. That assumption is usually some form of: people have this problem, and they will use or pay for this solution.
The idea was popularised by Eric Ries in
The Lean Startup

, which describes a build, measure, learn loop. You build something small, measure how people respond, learn from it, and use that learning to decide what to build next. The MVP is the first turn of that loop.
Why MVPs Get Overbuilt
Overbuilding rarely comes from carelessness. It usually comes from good intentions:
Fear that a simple product will look unprofessional
Every stakeholder adding one “essential” feature
Planning for scale before there are users to scale for
Building admin tools, settings, and integrations before they are needed
Confusing what the product could become with what it needs to prove first
Each addition seems reasonable on its own. Together they push launch back by months and make it harder to learn anything clear.
Step 1: Define the Core Job

Before listing features, write one sentence describing the job your product does for its users. For example: “Help small clinics fill cancelled appointments automatically.” That sentence becomes the filter for every scoping decision.
If a feature doesn’t directly help with the core job, it isn’t part of the MVP, however good the idea is.
Step 2: Map the Main User Journey

Sketch the shortest path a user takes to get value from your product, from first visit to the moment the core job is done. For a booking product that might be: sign up, connect a calendar, receive a cancellation, offer the slot, confirm the booking.
Every step on that path needs to work. Steps off the path can usually wait.
Step 3: Prioritize Features
List every feature idea the team has, then sort each one. A simple feature prioritization method is the MoSCoW technique:

cells: The core job fails without it
Valuable, but users can manage without it at first
Nice to have if time allows

children.text: Be strict. Most teams find their first “must have” list is two or three times too long. Admin dashboards, advanced settings, multiple user roles, and integrations can often be handled manually in the early days.
Step 4: Do Things That Don’t Scale

In the beginning, it is fine to handle some work by hand. Onboarding can be a call instead of a self serve flow. Reports can be sent by email instead of shown in a dashboard. Billing can start with simple invoices.
This approach lets you launch sooner and teaches you which tasks are worth automating, based on real usage instead of guesses.
Step 5: Design the Key Flow Properly

Doing less doesn’t mean doing it badly. The few screens in your MVP should be clear, fast, and trustworthy, because people judge credibility in seconds. A confusing MVP tells you nothing, because you can’t tell whether people rejected the idea or simply got lost.
Spend your design effort on the core journey: signing up, completing the main task, and seeing the result.
Step 6: Decide How You Will Measure Success
Product validation depends on knowing, before launch, which numbers will tell you whether the idea works. Choose one or two:
Activation: how many sign ups complete the core task
Retention: how many come back in the second or third week
Conversion: how many start paying, or agree to
Referral: how many invite someone else
Set up analytics for these from day one, so you learn from the very first user.
A Realistic MVP Development Process

cells: Core job, user journey, prioritized feature list
Tested prototype of the main flow

children.text: Timelines vary with complexity, but if your plan is far longer than this, revisit the must have list before anything else.
How to Scope an MVP: Common Mistakes to Avoid
Treating the MVP as a cheaper version of the final product
Skipping user research because “we already know what they want”
Building for thousands of users before you have ten
Launching without analytics
Leaving no time or budget for the second version
MVP Types That Validate Faster
An MVP doesn’t always have to be a full working product. Depending on what you need to learn, a lighter approach can answer the question in days or weeks instead of months.

cells: A page describes the product and asks people to sign up or join a waitlist
Whether people want it at all
You deliver the service manually for a few early customers
Whether the solution actually solves the problem
Users see a working product, but tasks are completed by people behind the scenes
Whether the experience works before automating it
A real product that does only the core job
Whether people use and return to it

children.text: Many successful products started with one of the lighter options, then built a single feature MVP once demand was clear.
How to Know When Your MVP Is Ready to Launch

An MVP is ready when a real user can complete the core job from start to finish without help, the experience feels trustworthy, and you can measure what happens. It doesn’t need every edge case covered or every nice to have feature. If you keep delaying launch to add one more thing, return to your core job sentence and ask whether the addition really changes what you will learn.

A short pre launch checklist helps: the core journey works on desktop and mobile, analytics events fire for each key step, there is a simple way for users to send feedback, and someone on the team is ready to respond to early users quickly. Those first conversations are often the most valuable data an MVP produces.
How a Focused MVP Supports SEO and AI Search

A focused product is also easier to explain. When your MVP solves one clear problem, your landing page can describe it in plain, specific language that matches what people search for and what AI answer tools look for when recommending solutions. Clear positioning from day one helps the right early users find you, which is exactly what an MVP needs.
Learn more about how we approach this on our
MVP development
page.

body.text: Planning an MVP and not sure what to cut? We help founders scope, design, and launch focused first versions.
body.label: Start a Project

faq.q: What is an MVP?
faq.a: A minimum viable product is the smallest version of a product that can test your most important assumption with real users. It does one job well enough that people can use it and give you meaningful feedback.

faq.q: How long should it take to build an MVP?
faq.a: Many MVPs can be designed and built in roughly two to four months. If your plan takes much longer, the scope is usually too big for a first version.

faq.q: How many features should an MVP have?
faq.a: There is no fixed number. It should include only the features needed to complete the core job end to end. For many products that is a handful of screens and one main workflow.

faq.q: Should an MVP look unfinished?
faq.a: No. An MVP should do less, not look worse. A focused product with a clean, trustworthy design gives you more reliable feedback than a rough one.

faq.q: What is the difference between an MVP and a prototype?
faq.a: A prototype simulates the product so you can test ideas and usability. An MVP is a working product that real users can use for real, which lets you test demand and behaviour.

faq.q: What happens after the MVP launches?
faq.a: You measure how people use it, talk to early users, and decide what to improve, add, or remove. The MVP is the start of learning, not the end of the project.

title: SEO And AEO: Getting Found In Search And AI Answers
excerpt: Learn how SEO and AEO work together, what answer engine optimization changes, and the practical steps that help your content appear in search and AI answers.

mainImage.alt: Search results and AI answer panels on a screen

children.text: Search is changing. People still type questions into Google, but many now get their answer from an AI generated summary, a chat assistant, or a voice assistant before they ever click a link. That shift has introduced a new term alongside SEO: answer engine optimization, or AEO. Understanding how SEO and AEO work together is now part of being found online.
The good news is that AEO doesn’t replace what already works. The habits that make content clear and useful for people also make it easy for search engines and AI tools to understand.
What Are SEO and AEO?
Search engine optimization (SEO) is the practice of helping your pages rank in search results so people click through to your website. It covers technical health, content quality, and authority.

Answer engine optimization (AEO) is the practice of shaping your content so search engines and AI assistants can understand it, quote it, and recommend it when they answer a question directly. It focuses on clear questions, direct answers, and trustworthy sources.
A closely related term, generative engine optimization (GEO), describes the same idea for generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, and Google’s AI Overviews.
How Search Has Changed

cells: Links plus AI summaries and direct answers
Questions matched to clear, trusted answers
Being cited or mentioned also builds visibility
Search engines, chat assistants, and voice tools all answer questions

children.text: Clicks still matter, but visibility now also includes being the source an AI tool trusts enough to quote.
Why SEO Is Still the Foundation

AI answer tools don’t invent their knowledge from nothing. Many draw on content that search engines have already crawled, indexed, and ranked. If your site is slow, hard to crawl, or thin on useful content, it is unlikely to be chosen as a source.
That means the fundamentals still come first:
Pages that load quickly and work well on mobile
A clean sitemap and sensible internal links
No accidental noindex tags or blocked pages
Content that genuinely answers the questions your audience asks
1. Answer One Clear Question Per Page
Pages that try to cover everything often answer nothing well. Give each important page a clear purpose and a question it answers. Put the direct answer near the top, then go into detail.
A useful test is to read your first paragraph on its own. If it would make sense quoted in an AI answer, you are on the right track.
2. Use Structure Machines Can Follow
Answer engine optimization depends on structure as much as words:
One clear H1 and descriptive H2 and H3 headings
Short paragraphs focused on one idea each
Lists for steps and tables for comparisons
Definitions that start with “X is…” for key terms
A short FAQ section that answers common follow up questions
3. Add Structured Data

Structured data for SEO uses JSON-LD markup to tell search engines exactly what a page is: an article, an organization, a service, a product, or a set of questions and answers. It helps crawlers interpret your content with less guesswork.

Be realistic about what it does. Since 2023, Google shows FAQ rich results only for a small set of well known government and health websites, and it has retired HowTo rich results. Structured data is still valuable for understanding, but it isn’t a guaranteed route to special search features.
4. Show Experience and Expertise

Search engines and AI tools increasingly look for signals that content comes from people who know the subject. Google’s guidance on helpful content refers to experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trust.
Name the author or team and explain their experience
Share real examples, processes, and lessons from your own work
Keep important pages up to date and show when they were last updated
Link to reliable sources when you state facts
5. Build Consistent Brand Signals

AI tools form a picture of your brand from everything they can find: your website, your business profiles, reviews, and mentions on other sites. Describe what you do in the same clear terms everywhere, so tools can connect your name with the right topics and questions.
SEO and AEO Checklist

cells: Mentions and citations in AI answers

children.text: How to Write Content AI Tools Can Quote
AI answer tools tend to quote passages that are self contained, specific, and clearly structured. A simple pattern works well for most informational pages:
Start with a direct answer.
Open the section with one or two sentences that fully answer the question.
Add context.
Explain why the answer is true, when it applies, and any important exceptions.
Give specifics.
Include numbers, steps, examples, or comparisons that make the answer useful.
Close the loop.
Link to related pages that go deeper, so both readers and crawlers can follow the topic.

For example, a page about pricing should state the price range in the first lines, then explain what affects it, rather than leading with a long introduction about the company. The same principle applies to service pages, guides, and FAQs.

Write in plain language and keep terminology consistent. If you call something a “discovery phase” on one page and a “scoping sprint” on another, both people and machines may struggle to connect the two.
Keep Important Pages Fresh

Outdated content is one of the quickest ways to lose trust with readers, search engines, and AI tools alike. Prices change, processes improve, and statistics age. Review your most important pages at least twice a year:
Check that facts, figures, and examples are still accurate
Update screenshots and references to tools or platforms
Add answers to new questions customers have started asking
Show a visible “last updated” date when you make meaningful changes
Remove or redirect pages that are no longer relevant
Fresh, accurate pages are more likely to be ranked, cited, and recommended, and they are more useful to the people who find them.
How to Measure SEO and AEO Results
Use Google Search Console to track impressions, clicks, and the queries you appear for
Watch referral traffic from AI tools in your analytics, where it is identified
Every month or two, ask the main AI assistants the questions your customers ask and note whether your brand is mentioned and how
Track which pages earn links and citations from other sites
Common Mistakes to Avoid
Writing for algorithms instead of people
Publishing many thin pages instead of fewer thorough ones
Ignoring technical SEO because “AI search is different”
Hiding the answer below long introductions
Letting important pages go out of date
Why Getting This Right Matters Now

AI answers are becoming a normal part of how people research products and services. Brands that are clear, consistent, and genuinely helpful are the ones these tools can understand and recommend. The work is the same work that has always produced good SEO, done with more attention to structure and clarity.

page.

faq.q: What is the difference between SEO and AEO?
faq.a: SEO helps your pages rank in search results so people click through to your site. AEO helps your content be understood, quoted, and recommended when a search engine or AI assistant answers a question directly.

faq.q: Does AEO replace SEO?
faq.a: No. AEO builds on SEO. AI answer tools still rely on content that can be crawled, indexed, and trusted, so strong technical SEO and helpful content remain the foundation.

faq.q: What is generative engine optimization?
faq.a: Generative engine optimization, or GEO, is a related term for shaping content so generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity understand your brand and cite it in their answers.

faq.q: Does FAQ schema still help?
faq.a: Since 2023, Google shows FAQ rich results only for a small set of well known government and health websites. Structured data can still help search engines understand a page, but most business sites will not get FAQ snippets.

faq.q: How do I know if AI tools mention my brand?
faq.a: Ask the main AI assistants the questions your customers ask, note whether and how your brand appears, and repeat the check every month or two. Also watch for referral traffic from AI tools in your analytics.

faq.q: How long does it take to see results?
faq.a: Technical fixes can show in search data within weeks. Building the authority that leads to consistent rankings and AI mentions usually takes several months of steady, high quality content.

title: Using AI Tools In A Design Workflow
excerpt: Build an AI design workflow that works: which tasks AI speeds up, where human judgement still matters, and how to adopt AI tools safely in your team.

mainImage.alt: Designer working with AI tools on a laptop

children.text: AI tools are now part of most design teams’ day. Used well, they remove hours of repetitive work and give designers more time for the parts of the job that need judgement. Used carelessly, they produce generic work and new risks. Building a sensible AI design workflow means knowing where these tools help, where they don’t, and how to use them responsibly.
This guide covers the practical uses we have found most valuable, the limits to watch for, and a simple way to introduce AI into your team.
What Is an AI Design Workflow?

An AI design workflow is a design process that uses AI tools to support specific tasks, such as research synthesis, copywriting, idea generation, and quality checks, while designers stay responsible for decisions and outcomes.

It isn’t about handing the whole job to a machine. It is about identifying the slow, repetitive steps around the real design work and using AI to speed them up, so the team can spend more time understanding users and solving problems.
Why Design Teams Are Adopting AI

Design work includes a surprising amount of repetitive effort: summarising interview notes, writing variations of microcopy, resizing assets, documenting components, and checking screens for missing states. These tasks matter, but they rarely need deep creative thinking.

AI tools for designers are good at exactly this kind of work. They can produce a first draft in seconds, which a designer then reviews, edits, and improves. The time saved goes back into research, iteration, and craft.
Where AI Helps Most
AI UX Research Support

After a round of user interviews, AI can help group notes into themes, pull out representative quotes, and draft a first summary. A researcher still checks the summary against the recordings, but the first draft takes minutes instead of hours. AI can also help draft interview guides and survey questions for a researcher to refine.
Writing and Microcopy

Button labels, error messages, empty states, and onboarding hints are often written last and in a hurry. AI is useful for generating several options quickly, which a designer or writer then edits to match the brand’s voice and the product’s context.
Ideas and Early Concepts
Generative AI design tools can create quick visual directions for moodboards, early layout ideas, and placeholder imagery. They are a starting point for discussion, not finished work.
Quality Checks and Edge Cases
Describe a screen or flow and ask what could go wrong: no data, slow connection, an error, a very long name, a first time user. AI is good at listing edge cases a busy team might miss.
Design Automation and Documentation

AI features in design and development tools can help rename layers, generate component descriptions, draft documentation, and translate design tokens into code formats. This kind of design automation keeps systems tidy with less manual effort.
AI Tasks at a Glance

cells: Checks against recordings and decides what matters
Edits for voice, clarity, and context
Chooses a direction that fits the brand and users
Designs the right response for each
Reviews accuracy and keeps it current

children.text: Where AI Doesn’t Help
AI has clear limits, and knowing them protects the quality of your work:
Understanding real users.
AI can summarise what people said, but it can’t replace talking to them and watching them use your product.
Brand judgement.
Generated work tends toward the average. A distinctive brand needs deliberate, opinionated choices.
Accessibility decisions.
AI suggestions can miss contrast, focus order, or screen reader issues. They need proper checking.
Accountability.
Someone on the team must own every decision that ships.
Risks to Manage
Before adopting any tool widely, agree how your team will handle a few important risks:
Client and user data.
Check your agreements, privacy rules, and the tool’s data settings before pasting research notes or customer information. Remove personal details wherever you can.
Originality and rights.
Generated images and text can resemble existing work, and the legal position differs by country and tool. Review outputs carefully.
Accuracy.
AI can state incorrect information confidently. Verify facts before they reach a client or a live product.
Sameness.
Over relying on the same tools can make work look like everyone else’s.
How to Introduce AI Into Your Team
Pick one repetitive task that takes too long, such as summarising interview notes.
Try one tool on that task for a few weeks.
Agree simple rules on data, review, and when not to use AI.
Compare time saved and quality against your usual process.
Share what worked, then move on to the next task.
Starting small makes it easy to see real value and avoids adding tools nobody uses.
How We Use AI at Waymarks

In our projects, AI helps us move faster through research synthesis, first drafts of copy, and quality checks. The core of the work hasn’t changed: understanding the problem, talking to users, designing with intent, and testing with real people. AI makes the supporting work lighter so more time goes into the parts clients actually notice.
Measuring Whether AI Is Actually Helping
It is easy to feel faster with AI without being faster. Track a few simple measures before and after you introduce a tool:

cells: Hours on the task before and after using AI
How much AI output had to be rewritten or corrected
Review feedback, usability findings, or client comments
How many team members still use the tool after a month

children.text: If a tool saves time but creates extra rework, the gain may be smaller than it looks. If people quietly stop using it, find out why before rolling it out further.
A Simple AI Usage Policy for Design Teams

A one page policy prevents most problems. It should cover which tools are approved, what data must never be entered, how AI generated work is reviewed before it reaches clients, and when to tell clients that AI was used. Keep it short, review it every few months, and update it as tools and regulations change.
Skills Designers Need Alongside AI
As AI takes on more routine production work, the skills that set designers apart become more important, not less:
Research and empathy.
Understanding real people, their context, and their constraints
Critical review.
Spotting what is wrong, generic, or inaccessible in generated output
Problem framing.
Asking the right question before generating any answers
Communication.
Explaining design decisions to clients, developers, and stakeholders
Systems thinking.
Keeping products consistent as they grow
Teams that invest in these skills get far more from AI tools, because they know what good looks like and can steer the output toward it.

The most effective designers we work with treat AI as a fast, tireless junior collaborator: useful for first drafts and repetitive tasks, but always guided, checked, and improved by someone who understands the user and the business.
How an AI Design Workflow Supports SEO and AI Search

AI can also help teams produce clearer, better structured content, such as consistent headings, plain language summaries, and complete FAQ sections, which makes pages easier for search engines and AI answer tools to understand. The same rule applies as everywhere else: people review and edit the output, so the content stays accurate, specific, and genuinely useful.

faq.q: Will AI replace designers?
faq.a: AI is changing how designers work, not removing the need for them. Understanding people, making trade offs, and taking responsibility for a product still require human judgement.

faq.q: What are the best AI tools for designers?
faq.a: Most teams start with a general AI assistant for writing and summarising, plus the AI features already built into the design tools they use. The best tool is the one that solves a specific, repeated task in your workflow.

faq.q: Is it safe to put client data into AI tools?
faq.a: Only if the tool and its settings meet your client agreements and privacy rules. Remove personal data where possible, and check whether the tool uses your inputs for training.

faq.q: Can AI do user research?
faq.a: AI can help plan studies, summarise notes, and spot themes, but it cannot replace talking to and observing real users. Synthetic or AI generated users are not a substitute for real research.

faq.q: How do we start using AI in our design team?
faq.a: Pick one repetitive task, try one tool on it for a few weeks, agree simple rules on data and review, and share what worked before expanding.

faq.q: Does AI generated design work have copyright issues?
faq.a: It can. Generated images and text may resemble existing work, and the legal position varies by country and tool. Review outputs carefully and check the tool’s terms before using them in client work.
